subject: Agriculture
title: Corn: America's Crop
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Corn: America's Crop.

hook.text: Corn doesn't exist in the wild. It was engineered by indigenous people from a grass called teosinte.

buildup.text: Teosinte has tiny ears with a dozen hard seeds. Ancient farmers selectively bred larger ears over thousands of years.

discovery.text: Modern corn ears have 800 kernels—a transformation so extreme that scientists debated whether corn was even natural.

twist.text: Today, most US corn isn't eaten by people. It goes to ethanol fuel, animal feed, and high-fructose corn syrup.

climax.text: Corn is the most produced grain on Earth—over one billion tons yearly. It defines American agriculture.

punchline.text: Humans made corn. Without us, it can't even drop its own seeds.

quiz.question: What is corn's wild ancestor?
options: Teosinte, a grass with tiny ears

details.summary: Corn, or maize, is the most-produced grain in the world and the backbone of American agriculture. This topic covers corn's domestication from teosinte, its incredible versatility as food, feed, and fuel, and its outsized role in global trade and food systems.
details.whyItMatters: Corn is in everything from livestock feed to ethanol to high-fructose syrup. Its price and supply ripple through global food markets, making it one of the most strategically important crops.
takeaways: The US alone produces over 30% of the world's corn supply
Only about 10% of US corn is eaten directly; most goes to feed and ethanol
Corn was domesticated from teosinte in Mexico around 9,000 years ago

faq.question: Why is corn considered America's most important crop?
faq.answer: Corn dominates US agriculture with over 90 million acres planted annually. It feeds livestock, produces ethanol fuel, generates high-fructose corn syrup and industrial products, and is a major export commodity affecting global food prices.

faq.question: How was corn domesticated from a wild grass?
faq.answer: Indigenous peoples in southern Mexico selectively bred teosinte—a grass with tiny, hard kernels—over thousands of years, gradually producing the large cobs and soft kernels of modern maize through ongoing human selection.
